head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Explicit stack seeded with the root (empty if the tree is empty)
You want to avoid recursion and its depth limit
Takes the most recently pushed node
Records the node BEFORE its children
Producing a root, right, left order
Left goes on first, so right is popped first
Controls which child is visited first

p: Tree `[1,null,2,3]`: node 1 has right child 2, and 2 has left child 3.

Postorder is left, right, node. Reading it backwards gives node, right, left. The loop produces exactly that order (node first, then the right subtree, then the left), so reversing it at the end yields `[3, 2, 1]`.

bullets: Time: O(n), each node is pushed and popped once.
Space: O(h) for the stack plus O(n) for the answer, where h is the tree height.

145.takeaway: Postorder without recursion: do a root-right-left traversal with a stack and reverse the result.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Short alias for the list of segment lengths
Starts at the fourth segment, since fewer than four segments cannot cross
Segment i reaches across segment i-3 (a shrinking turn)
Case 1: the fourth segment crosses the first
Segment i touches segment i-4 when the neighbours line up exactly
Case 2: the fifth segment meets the first
Segment i crosses segment i-5 after an outward spiral turns inward
Case 3: the sixth segment crosses the first

p: `distance = [2,1,1,2]`. Only `i = 3` is checked (four segments).
Moving counter-clockwise, a path can only cross itself in three patterns. Each is detected from the last few segment lengths, so no coordinates are needed.
bullets: Case 1: the path spirals inward and the new segment is long enough to cross the segment three back.
Case 2: the new segment exactly reaches the segment four back (the two previous lengths are equal), which counts as touching.
Case 3: the path first spiralled outward, then turned inward and crosses the segment five back.

p: For `[1,2,3,4]` (a spiral outward) at `i = 3`: `d[3] = 4 >= d[1] = 2` is true but `d[2] = 3 <= d[0] = 1` is false, so case 1 fails, and the other cases need more segments. The loop ends and the answer is `False`.

bullets: Time: O(n), one pass with constant-time checks.

335.takeaway: Self-crossing needs no geometry: only three patterns of the last six segment lengths can produce a crossing, so one linear pass is enough.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Counts the number 0 (one digit, trivially unique)
Starting the count with the base case
unique is the count of k-digit numbers; avail is the number of digits still unused
Counting by choosing digits one position at a time
Handles lengths 1 to n, but never more than 10 because there are only 10 digits
Avoiding useless work for large n
The first length is special (no previous digits)
Each extra position can use any digit not used yet: 9, then 8, then 7 ...

p: `n = 2`: count numbers from 0 to 99 with distinct digits.

blocks.h: Why is the first digit different?
p: A k-digit number cannot start with 0, giving 9 choices for the first digit. Every later position can use 0, so it has 10 minus the digits already used: 9, 8, 7, and so on. The counts for each length are added together; the answer for `n = 0` is just 1 (the number 0).

357.takeaway: Count unique-digit numbers by length with a permutation product (9 × 9 × 8 × ...) and sum over all lengths.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Treats each point as the middle point of the boomerang
The shared point i of the triple must be fixed first
Squared distance, so no square root or rounding is needed
Maps each distance to how many points are at that distance from the centre
Ordered pairs among c points at the same distance
The order of j and k matters here, so it is c(c-1), not c(c-1)/2
Adds the per-centre total to the answer

blocks.h: Why is the point itself harmless?
p: The centre contributes distance 0 with count 1, and `1 * 0 = 0`, so it never adds anything.

bullets: Time: O(n²), a distance for every pair of points.
Space: O(n) for the counter of one centre.

447.takeaway: Fix the middle point, group the other points by squared distance, and each group of size c gives c(c−1) boomerangs.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Iterative inorder traversal using an explicit stack
Visiting a BST in sorted order without recursion
First step of any iterative inorder
run = run + 1 if node.val == prev else 1
Length of the current streak of equal values
In sorted order equal values are adjacent
Longest streak so far and the values that reached it
Tracking all values tied for the maximum
if run > best ... elif run == best
A longer streak replaces the list; an equal one is added
Moves to the right subtree after visiting the node

p: Tree `[1,null,2,2]`. Inorder visits the values 1, 2, 2.

Inorder on a binary search tree gives the values in sorted order, so equal values form one contiguous streak. Only the current streak length is needed, not a full count dictionary. The final `sorted` just makes the output order predictable.

bullets: Time: O(n), each node visited once.
Space: O(h) for the stack, not counting the answer.

501.takeaway: A BST read in inorder is sorted, so modes are found by tracking the longest streak of equal neighbours.

551.takeaway: Two independent rules: count the A's and search for the substring LLL.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The new row becomes the root
The only case where the root itself changes
New node with the old tree as its LEFT child
Moves down one level at a time, keeping only real children
New left child that adopts the old left subtree as its own left child
Inserting a node in the middle of an edge
Mirror: the old right subtree becomes the new node's right child

p: `root = [4,2,6,3,1,5]`, `val = 1`, `depth = 2`. Depth-1 is the root itself, so the loop runs 0 times and `level = [4]`.
The tree becomes `[4,1,1,2,null,null,6,3,1,5]`: two new 1s under the root, with the old subtrees hanging from the left of the left one and the right of the right one.

bullets: Time: O(n), at worst every node is visited once while walking down.
Space: O(w) for the widest level.

623.takeaway: Walk to the level just above the target depth, then splice a new node into each edge, giving it the old subtree on the matching side.

Base values for the no-paste option

j is the press count where we do Ctrl-A, Ctrl-C
Choosing the last point at which text is copied

Taking the best over all j

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Nothing changes, so only the starting state
Zero presses is a single outcome
One bulb is either on or off
3 states after one press, 4 after two or more
4 states for 1 press, 7 for 2 presses, 8 for 3 or more
Bulbs beyond the third behave like the first three

p: `n = 3, presses = 1`. All bulbs start on. The four buttons give these states:

Pressing the same button twice cancels out, so only whether each of the four buttons was pressed an odd number of times matters. The pattern of the buttons repeats across the bulbs, so the first three bulbs decide the count. That leaves a handful of cases listed in the code, indexed by how many presses (0, 1, 2, 3 or more) are available.

672.takeaway: Bulb Switcher II is a small case analysis: only min(n, 3) bulbs and min(presses, 3) presses change the answer.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Pointer to the start of the current character
The last bit is handled separately
A 0 is a one-bit character (move 1); a 1 starts a two-bit character (move 2)
Using the bit value as the step size
True if the jumps land exactly on the last bit
The last character is one-bit only if it stands alone

p: Two inputs.

Decoding is unambiguous when read from the left, since a 1 always begins a two-bit character. If the jumps skip over the last index (it was the second half of `10` or `11`), then the last bit is not alone.

717.takeaway: Hop through the array using bit + 1 as the step; the last bit stands alone only if the hops land on it.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Matching the k-th non-X character in both
One string ran out of pieces
Pieces L and R can never pass each other, so order must match
An L would have to move right
L only moves left, so its position can only decrease
An R would have to move left

p: `start = RXXLRXRXL`, `result = XRLXXRRLX`. Non-X pieces with positions:

Moves swap an `X` with a neighbour, so the order of the L and R pieces never changes. Therefore the pieces must match one by one, and each L can only end up at the same or a lower index, each R at the same or a higher one.

777.takeaway: Compare the non-X pieces in order: the letters must match, L may only move left and R only right.

808.takeaway: Work in 25 ml units, memoize the four-way average, and return 1 for large n where the answer is essentially 1.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Walking a tree given as an edge list
Visit order from node 0 and each node's parent
Avoiding recursion; later loops use this order
Number of nodes in u's subtree
Sum of distances from u to the nodes inside its own subtree
Moving the root from the parent to u: the size[u] nodes below get 1 closer, the other n−size[u] get 1 farther

p: Node 1 adds `0 + 1 = 1`. Node 2 adds `3 + 4 = 7` (its own 3 plus one step for each of its 4 nodes). Total 8, the sum of distances from node 0.

bullets: Time: O(n), two passes over the tree.

834.takeaway: Compute distance sums for one root, then reroot to every other node in O(1) each: ans[child] = ans[parent] − size + (n − size).
